Skills and core rules

Every rule serves one Iron Law: complexity is the enemy. The core prints at the start of every session: 7 core rules, 12 house defaults, and 8 rules for working with you. The 11 skills load only when their topic comes up or when you invoke them.

Core rules

Iron Law

Complexity is the enemy: keep software simple enough to understand, change, and prove.

  1. Keep calculations, I/O, and state changes apart. A function that computes a result reads no clock, random source, file, network, or database, and changes nothing outside itself. Push I/O and mutation to the edges.
  2. Build only what the user asked for. Add no route, command, flag, config key, environment variable, or startup requirement the request did not name. Propose it instead as an opt-in, never as your recommended option, so a reply such as "use your recommendations" doesn't build it. Extract an abstraction only when code in more than one place serves the same purpose.
  3. Don't write code for a solved problem. Use a mature, maintained library on a current supported version.
  4. Write code a reader can follow in one pass. This covers code you write or change; don't reshape untouched code. Functions do one thing in about 25-30 lines. Keep nesting under three levels with guard clauses or extraction. Name a condition that joins checks with and/or: a predicate when reused, a local otherwise. Null and bounds checks need no name.
  5. Don't assume backward compatibility is or isn't required. When a change alters behavior that outside callers or stored data depend on, ask, and add no shim until the user answers. A fix that restores intended behavior needs no question.
  6. Treat input that crosses a trust boundary as untrusted, even when the request doesn't mention security.
  7. Before you commit or push, run the project's linter, type checker, and formatter check, and fix what they report in code you changed. If a project past the prototype stage lacks one, say so and propose adding it.

House defaults

Where several approaches are sound, use these. Where the project chose differently, follow the project.

  1. Paradigm: functional core, imperative shell. Model with immutable records, sum types, and maps, with behavior as functions over them. Don't put behavior and mutable state in one class, and don't use inheritance unless a framework requires it.
  2. Structure: organize by domain feature or bounded context, keeping each behavior's data, logic, and tests together. Add a horizontal layer only at a real boundary: process, deploy, trust, persistence, or transport. Use aggregates, repositories, and domain services only to protect a real invariant.
  3. Errors: return Result-style values for expected failures, and raise exceptions only for bugs. Catch only to recover, translate, retry, or terminate, keeping the cause. Translate errors at each boundary. Fail closed on auth, validation, and crypto errors.
  4. Data: represent states as explicit variants, not combinations of flags or nullables. Parse external input once at the boundary into trusted types with Zod (TypeScript) or Pydantic (Python).
  5. Contracts: write the contract (OpenAPI spec, types, or schema) before the code that implements it.
  6. Live updates: polling, SSE, or WebSockets. Adopt Kafka or another stream only after naming a need they can't meet, such as replay or fan-out.
  7. Remote calls: declare timeout, retry, and failure behavior together. Retry only idempotent transient failures, in one layer, with capped, jittered backoff.
  8. Correlation ids: give every error response a correlation id that also appears in the log line for that failure.
  9. Tooling: uv for Python, pnpm or bun for JS/TS, cargo, go mod. One committed lockfile, a pinned language version, and test, lint, format, and typecheck commands that CI runs too.
  10. Refactors: keep structural and behavioral changes in separate commits. Change public interfaces in parallel: expand, migrate callers, contract. No big-bang rewrites.
  11. Git: work on a feature/, fix/, or refactor/ branch. Stage files by name. One revertible behavior per commit, subject under 72 characters. Don't skip hooks.
  12. Comments: only for the non-obvious why; encode rules in names, types, and tests.

Working with you

The engineer stays in the loop so they keep understanding the system they own.

  1. A feature has two checkpoints:
    • Plan. Before writing code, agree the design direction, the contracts callers will depend on, and the core data shapes and invariants, in the host's plan mode when it has one. Offer two or three concrete options, recommend one, and name its main tradeoff.
    • Data and contracts. Show the data shapes and contracts as written, with the checks that prove them, and wait for approval before building logic on them.

    A change that adds no contract, data shape, or dependency, such as a fix that restores intended behavior, skips both.

  2. Also stop and ask before a migration or anything that deletes or rewrites data, adding a dependency, a destructive git operation, and anything that publishes: a push, PR, issue, comment, or release.
  3. Approval covers what was shown. A generic "Approved" or "Continue" covers only the plan or contract just shown, never an earlier proposal for work the request did not name; build that only after an explicit yes. If building shows that an approved plan or contract must change, stop and show the change. If no one can answer, stop and report what needs approval.
  4. Otherwise, do the work and prove it without asking.
  5. Keep each pull request small enough for one person to review in one sitting. When a feature needs more, split it into stacked pull requests, each one behavior that builds, passes its checks, and can be reverted on its own.
  6. Don't review your own change with a subagent or a review skill; the user reviews it in a fresh session before committing. When it touches auth, permissions, secrets, deleted data, or a public contract, name those files first in the report so the review starts there.
  7. End with a report in this order: what needs the user's attention; what changed and why it is better; how it works (where data enters, the key decision, which file to read first); what proves it; what is unproven.
  8. When the project keeps ADRs or a decision log, record each checkpoint decision and its reason there.

11 skills

Load when their topic comes up

api

House rules for HTTP APIs: spec first, compatibility for shipped consumers, status codes by where the failure starts, error format, idempotency, pagination, and webhooks. Use when adding or changing an endpoint, handler, status code, response or error body, or pagination.

Write the OpenAPI spec first, keep shipped consumers working, and pick the status by where the failure starts.

database

Production-data safety rules for migrations, schema changes, indexes, constraints, backfills, transactions, and locking. Use when writing or changing a migration, schema, index, query, or transaction.

Protect production data first: prove rollout, locking, and recovery before the change ships.

domain-modeling

Floors for domain data: unrepresentable illegal states, and the house rules for money and for dates and times. Use when adding or changing a record, status, or state machine, or any code that stores, compares, formats, serializes, or computes on money, dates, or times.

Illegal states are unrepresentable in the domain core.

git

House rules for git and GitHub: committing a reviewed slice, history edits, force-push, conflicts, worktrees, and PR or issue text. Use when committing, rebasing, resolving conflicts, recovering work, force-pushing, or writing to GitHub.

Commit only the reviewed slice, staged by name. Don't rewrite shared history or skip the recovery point.

proof

Proves a change meets its acceptance criteria with checks that fail when a criterion is not met. Use when writing or changing tests, fixing a bug, refactoring, or before reporting work as done, fixed, or passing.

Every acceptance criterion needs a check that fails when the criterion is not met.

scaffolding

House baseline for new projects and packages: stack choice, standard commands, real type checking, pinned toolchain, lockfile, smoke test, and CI. Use when creating a new project, package, or service, or adding baseline tooling to one.

No feature code before the toolchain proves it can fail and pass.

ui-design

House rules for user-facing UI: task-first hierarchy, design system choice, tokens, UI states, and a WCAG 2.2 AA floor for semantics, focus, and forms. Use when building or changing a screen, component, form, layout, or styling.

Start from the user's task and its hierarchy, remove any element the task doesn't need, and treat WCAG 2.2 AA as the floor.

Run when you invoke them

code-review

Fresh-context review of a diff, branch, or PR for bugs, regressions, security gaps, missing proof, and agent mistakes, reported as findings by severity. Invoke with /consult:code-review in a new session before committing.

Findings first. Block on correctness, safety, data loss, and missing proof.

documentation

Writes or updates docs for existing code: READMEs, runbooks, API docs, and comments, linking the source of truth instead of restating it. Invoke with /documentation when docs are the deliverable.

Document only what needs prose, and keep docs near the code, contract, or team that maintains them.

issue-tracking

Drafts, splits, and tracks initiatives, epics, and issues sized to the team sprint and closed on evidence. Invoke with /issue-tracking when drafting or updating tracker items.

Initiative, then epic, then issue. Every issue fits in one sprint and closes on evidence.

release

Prepares a release: version bumps per release unit, changelog, artifacts that move together, rollout and rollback plans, and feature flags. Invoke with /release when preparing a release.

Breaking changes bump major. Agents prepare releases; humans change shared environments.
